What these planners carried in their mind's eye was certain aesthetic, what one might call a visual codification of modern rural production and community life. The problem with bureaucrats is they have no imagination; everything to them has to be mapped out. They like things that can be mapped out, that can be a blueprint. They like to brag about these things because that's how they see the world.

But real-world nature requires diversity and organic processes. So he gives examples of how the state transforms society. Before people would just come together and organize their communities according to their needs in a bottom-up process. But the state wants to create permanent cities where people are just in one place all the time, right? That's why you have cities.

Before it was natural for people to live on small farms and share stuff with other people to trade with each other. The problem with this is the state cannot tax you. What the state does is bring you to cities, make you work in a factory so it can tax you. The point of giving you a wage is so it can tax you to exploit you.

Property was once very common for people to share together. Now, there's all owned and controlled by the state. Resources are the same thing; before people just use resources according to needs but now the state wants to centralize these resources so it can tax and exploit people properly. So that's what a state proxy does.

What are the consequences of the overbureaucratization of society? Well, in America, while consumer goods like cars, clothing, and cell phones are going down, hospital services, schooling, and housing are going up. Why? Because these are monopolies controlled by bureaucrats. So with the overbureaucratization of society, it's almost impossible for middle-class people or anyone to have a good life.

Now, here's another really interesting chart. The black shows you the growth in the stock market. You think, wow, this is a good thing. But first of all, only 10% of people in the United States control most of the stocks—over 90%. The other issue is if you look at prices, yeah, it's gone up, but if you just turn and use gold to buy stocks, guess what? The price of stocks have gone down. That's a blue. If you use money to buy stocks, it goes up, but if you use gold to buy stocks, it goes down.

What this is telling us very simply is we are living in a lie. All this wealth generation is all a lie; it's not real. We just think it's real. We're living in a fairy land created by bureaucrats to fool us into believing that we are prosperous. The amount of gold you can buy with stocks has gone down. And so the blue is the gold, the black is money. Money isn't worth anything.

Another problem that bureaucratization has created is people don't want to work anymore. In America, this is called quite quitting; in China, it's called tonging or banan—lying flat, let it rot. People don't want to work anymore because it's pointless to work in a bureaucracy where leaders don't care and organizations need you only as a machine. You feel alienated, told what to do with no ability to negotiate or rise from the bureaucracy.

You're being asked to work too much; you feel like just a machine. So the way you rebel is by lying flat or quite quitting. Your overbureaucratization of society means that people now have become more lazy, more complacent, and more indifferent. And what this also means is that democracy is declining because people's voice and power are declining.

You can see that people feel as though democracy is in decline. In fact, experts estimate that the capacity for people to participate in politics and influence politics has declined rapidly over the past 10 years.
